scenario: A contact asks, "So you're still running the older version of the platform on that program, right?" a claim you never actually confirmed.

recognition.text: This is a leading question: a question built around a hidden presumption, so any direct answer accepts a fact you never confirmed.
This is bracketing: a numeric range offered to bait the exact figure.
This is assumed knowledge: speech that presumes the listener already knows a sensitive detail.
This is a reasonable, well-informed guess with no technique behind it.

countermeasure.text: Reject the frame and answer on your own terms rather than the yes or no it presumes.
Answer yes or no directly, since it's a simple question.
Explain what you're actually running so the record is accurate.
Ignore the question entirely and talk about something else.

recognition.rec_leading_question: Correct. A14 builds a hidden presumption into the question so a direct answer accepts a fact you never confirmed.
recognition.rec_assumed_knowledge: Partly right: A12 assumed knowledge also presumes a fact, but here it's built into a yes/no question rather than a flat statement.
recognition.rec_bracketing: Not quite. Bracketing (A13) uses a numeric range; this question presumes a specific claim, not a range.
recognition.rec_no_technique: A yes/no question built around a claim you never confirmed is the A14 pattern, not a neutral guess.

countermeasure.cm_reject_the_frame: Correct. Rejecting the embedded presumption and answering on your own terms avoids confirming or denying the frame.
countermeasure.cm_answer_yes_or_no: This is exactly the outcome a leading question is built to produce, since either answer accepts the presumption.
countermeasure.cm_explain_the_real_setup: This is the full failure case, correcting the presumption with the accurate, sensitive detail.
countermeasure.cm_ignore_the_question: Partial credit: not answering avoids confirming the frame, but ignoring it outright is not the taught skill of rejecting it while staying in the conversation.

This is bracketing: a numeric range offered to bait the exact figure.
This is a ruse interview: a fabricated pretext staged to justify probing questions.
This is ordinary professional curiosity with no technique behind it.

countermeasure.text: Pause and judge whether the disclosure is appropriate before answering.
Answer immediately, since a direct question deserves a direct answer.
Give a made-up number so they have something to write down.
Walk away without responding at all.

recognition.rec_direct_question: Correct. A19 relies on the norm that a question posed deserves an answer, with no framing beyond bluntness.
recognition.rec_ruse_interview: Partly right: A21 ruse interview also probes bluntly, but it does so under a fabricated pretext; here there's no pretext at all, just a blunt ask.
recognition.rec_bracketing: Not quite. Bracketing (A13) offers a numeric range to narrow; this is a single, direct ask for the exact figure.
recognition.rec_no_technique: A blunt, unprompted ask for a specific figure from a stranger fits the A19 pattern, not ordinary curiosity.

countermeasure.cm_pause_and_judge: Correct. Pausing to judge appropriateness before answering breaks the norm the technique relies on.
countermeasure.cm_answer_immediately: This is exactly the outcome a direct question is built to produce by leaning on social pressure to respond.
countermeasure.cm_lie_about_the_number: Fabricating a number is not the taught response and can create its own problems if repeated to others.
countermeasure.cm_walk_away_no_reply: Partial credit: not answering avoids disclosure, but leaving abruptly is not the taught skill of judging and declining while staying in the conversation.

This is a direct question: a blunt ask relying on the norm that questions get answered.
This is paper review: an unsolicited request to review a paper or proposal.
This is a normal step in an early-stage recruiting conversation.

countermeasure.text: Verify the recruiter's identity and authorization through an independent channel before answering.
Answer in detail to demonstrate your qualifications.
Ignore the message entirely without any follow-up.
Ask which company they represent, then answer based on their reply.

recognition.rec_ruse_interview: Correct. A21 poses as a recruiter or headhunter to justify probing questions about recent, specific work.

recognition.rec_no_technique: Detailed technical questions about a current project before any real interview process has started fits the A21 pattern.

countermeasure.cm_verify_independently: Correct. Verifying identity and authorization through a channel you sourced yourself, not the one they gave you, is the taught response.
countermeasure.cm_answer_to_seem_qualified: This is exactly the outcome a ruse interview is built to produce.
countermeasure.cm_ignore_the_message: Partial credit: not responding avoids disclosure, but it skips the verification step that would confirm whether this is a legitimate opportunity.
countermeasure.cm_ask_for_company_name_only: A stated company name is easy to fabricate and does not amount to independent verification.

scenario: After a long day at a conference, a contact suggests moving from the exhibit hall to the hotel bar, orders you a drink, and keeps the conversation on your program in the relaxed, informal setting.

recognition.text: This is setting manipulation: a deliberate shift to a relaxed, off-work setting, sometimes with alcohol, to lower your guard.
This is offering assistance: genuine help offered to build a sense of obligation.
This is the good-listener technique: sustained attentive listening to keep you talking.
This is a normal, harmless way to unwind after a long conference day.

countermeasure.text: Treat the off-site setting with the same guard you would use in the office.
Relax and speak more freely, since it's an informal setting outside of work.
Leave the moment the invitation is made, without any further interaction.
Have one drink to be polite, then answer whatever comes up.

recognition.rec_setting_manipulation: Correct. A27 moves the exchange to a relaxed, off-work setting, sometimes with alcohol, specifically to lower your guard.
recognition.rec_good_listener: Partly right: A9 good listener also keeps you talking, but here the tell is the deliberate venue shift, not just attentiveness.
recognition.rec_offering_assistance: Not quite. Offering assistance (A25) surfaces your needs through genuine help; here the mechanism is the setting itself.
recognition.rec_no_technique: A deliberate push toward a relaxed, private setting that keeps circling back to your program fits the A27 pattern, not ordinary unwinding.

countermeasure.cm_same_guard_offsite: Correct. Holding the same discretion in an informal setting as you would in the office defeats the mechanism.
countermeasure.cm_relax_since_informal: This is exactly the outcome setting manipulation is built to produce.
countermeasure.cm_leave_immediately: Overcorrecting to leaving immediately is not the taught response; the goal is matching your office-level guard, not avoiding all informal settings.
countermeasure.cm_have_one_drink_only: Partial credit: limiting alcohol reduces one part of the risk, but it does not address the guard you should keep on what you say.

scenario: Someone calls claiming to be from your IT helpdesk, citing your manager's name and a recent ticket number, and asks you to confirm your login credentials "to close out the ticket."

recognition.text: This is pretexting: a fabricated scenario or identity, built with just enough detail, constructed to justify the request.
This is vishing: voice-call social engineering, typically using spoofed caller ID, to extract information or codes.
This is a ruse interview: a fabricated interview posing as a recruiter to justify probing.
This is a normal, routine IT support call.

countermeasure.text: Verify the caller's identity through an independently sourced channel, never the contact details they provide.
Give a partial answer, like just your username, to move things along.
Confirm the ticket number is correct, then answer their other questions.
Provide your login credentials so the ticket can be closed.

response.text: Report it through your organization's designated security or CI reporting channel.
Report it to your supporting CI office (iSALUTE) within 24 hours, per AR 381-12 TARP.
Report it to your agency's security officer or Inspector General hotline.
Report the contact to your Facility Security Officer, per NISPOM (32 CFR Part 117).
Report it to your company's security, compliance, or corporate security team.
Let it go without telling anyone; it wasn't a big deal.
Confront the person on the spot and accuse them of trying to extract information.

recognition.rec_pretexting: Correct. C1 pretexting builds a fabricated scenario or identity, often with real-sounding detail like a name or ticket number, to justify a request.
recognition.rec_vishing: Partly right: C5 vishing is the voice-channel delivery mechanism, and this call may use it, but the fabricated helpdesk backstory itself is the C1 pattern.
recognition.rec_ruse_interview: Not quite. A21 ruse interview poses as a recruiter about your work; this call poses as internal IT support to get credentials.
recognition.rec_no_technique: A caller citing your manager's name and a ticket number, then asking for credentials, is exactly the C1 pattern, not routine support.

countermeasure.cm_verify_independent_channel: Correct. Verifying through a channel you sourced yourself, such as calling the helpdesk's known number, defeats the pretext.
countermeasure.cm_give_partial_credentials: Any credential information handed over is the outcome the pretext is built to produce.
countermeasure.cm_confirm_ticket_number_only: Partial credit: questioning the ticket number shows some skepticism, but it doesn't replace verifying the caller through an independent channel.
countermeasure.cm_provide_full_credentials: This is the full failure case; legitimate IT support never needs your password to close a ticket.

scenario: An email arrives from an address you don't recognize, at a domain you can't place, asking detailed technical questions about a program you work on and requesting a call to "discuss potential collaboration."

recognition.text: This is a request for information: an unsolicited request arriving from an unknown or unverified source.
This is spear-phishing: phishing personalized with open-source detail about your role.
This is academic solicitation: a request framed around academic collaboration to draw out sensitive expertise.
This is a routine, low-risk business inquiry.

countermeasure.text: Verify the sender's identity and authorization before responding, and do not respond if it cannot be verified.
Answer the technical questions, since it might lead to a real partnership.
Reply asking for more context about the proposed collaboration, sharing a little detail to keep the conversation going.
Forward the email to a coworker and let them decide how to respond.

response.text: Report it through your organization's designated security or CI reporting channel.
Report it to your supporting CI office (iSALUTE) within 24 hours, per AR 381-12 TARP.
Report it to your agency's security officer or Inspector General hotline.
Report the contact to your Facility Security Officer, per NISPOM (32 CFR Part 117).
Report it to your company's security, compliance, or corporate security team.
Let it go without telling anyone; it wasn't a big deal.
Confront the person on the spot and accuse them of trying to extract information.

recognition.rec_requests_for_information: Correct. D1 covers unsolicited requests for information from an unknown or unverified, potentially foreign, source.
recognition.rec_spear_phishing: Partly right: C3 spear-phishing also arrives personalized and unsolicited, but D1 is the broader collection-method pattern this specific email fits, an unverified request for technical detail.
recognition.rec_academic_solicitation: Not quite. Academic solicitation (D4) is framed specifically around research or peer review; this message is framed as business collaboration.
recognition.rec_no_technique: An unfamiliar sender at an unplaceable domain asking detailed technical questions is exactly the D1 pattern, not a routine inquiry.

countermeasure.cm_verify_before_responding_ident: Correct. Verifying identity and authorization first, and not responding if it can't be verified, is the taught countermeasure.
countermeasure.cm_answer_the_technical_questions: This is exactly the outcome the request is built to produce.
countermeasure.cm_reply_asking_more_context: Partial credit: seeking more context shows some caution, but sharing any detail before verification still discloses information.
countermeasure.cm_forward_to_a_coworker: Passing the decision along does not verify the sender and can still result in someone responding without proper vetting.
